summary: An excerpt from a fiction novel (Book 6, part 94) in which first-person narrator Cas Russell is questioned by a federal agent named Jones. Cas reasons that the Feds identified her through inquiries among disreputable contacts, since her description as a short, brown, female person narrowed the possibilities. Jones demands her real name, accuses her of using an alias, and warns that she is close to moving from witness to perpetrator in the Halliday matter. Cas insists Cas Russell is her real name, bristles at the questioning, and admits she tracked down and rescued Professor Halliday, with Jones demanding a detailed account.
one_line: Cas Russell is interrogated by federal agent Jones about her real name and her role in rescuing Professor Halliday.
key_facts: Jones says of Cas Russell: 'Cas Russell,' she said, meaning the agent has identified the narrator by that name.
The narrator reasons that being a foot shorter, brown, and female meant a few questions in the right corners would get the Feds a correct ID.
Jones asks, 'Now what's your real name?' and the narrator answers 'Cas Russell is my real name.'
Jones responds with the instant denial 'Bullshit,' which the narrator calls a slap to the face.
The narrator offers to take a polygraph, saying she could control her physiological responses enough to fool the machine but was telling the truth.
The narrator says that if she burned an alias every job she'd never be able to build up a client base.
The narrator sarcastically claims her name is Bridget Twitwaffle and tells Jones to put it in her fancy computers.
Jones tells the narrator she is a fingernail's width away from going from 'witness' to 'perpetrator.'
Jones says that if the Feds only care about the narrator in reference to Halliday, that could be a very good thing.
Jones demands to know what happened in there, and the narrator answers that she tracked down Professor Halliday and rescued her.
The narrator's internal reaction to the questioning is one of annoyance and impatience, and she studies the ceiling to avoid Jones's intense stare.
